Case Vignette: Alex

Alex sits across from me with their hands folded tightly in their lap, shoulders drawn up toward their ears. They're a software engineer at a mid-sized tech company, someone accustomed to problem-solving and logic, yet they describe their current life as feeling fundamentally broken in ways code cannot fix.

Three years ago, Alex was driving home from work around 9 PM when they were pulled over for a broken taillight. They remember the officer approaching the window, remember the sudden brightness of the flashlight, remember their hands trembling as they reached for their license. What they struggle to articulate-what makes them pause and look away-is what happened next. The officer claimed Alex made a sudden movement. There was shouting. Alex was pulled from the car, thrown against the hood, handcuffed. The officer's knee pressed into their back. Alex kept saying they hadn't done anything wrong, kept trying to explain, but the officer's voice only got louder. When backup arrived, Alex was arrested on charges that were later dropped. The entire interaction lasted perhaps eight minutes, though Alex describes it as both instantaneous and endless.

Since that night, Alex's world has contracted. They still go to work-the routine helps, the logic of programming provides temporary refuge-but the drive there involves careful route planning to avoid that intersection. Some days, when a notification on their phone makes a sharp sound, or when a colleague speaks loudly during a meeting, Alex's body floods with adrenaline. Their heart races. Their breathing becomes shallow. Once, during a code review, a manager approached from behind, and Alex startled so violently they nearly fell from their chair. The embarrassment lingered longer than the fear.

At night, sleep has become unreliable. Alex lies awake, replaying the encounter, cataloging everything they might have done differently-moved slower, spoken differently, been a different person. On the nights sleep does come, there are dreams: being trapped, unable to move, unable to make anyone understand. They wake gasping, their spouse beside them, worried and helpless.

Alex's marriage has strained under the weight of this. Their spouse tries to be supportive, but there's a distance now. Intimacy has become difficult. When their spouse touches them unexpectedly, Alex flinches. They've noticed their spouse has started announcing their presence before entering a room, learned to move slowly and deliberately around them. The guilt of this-of making their partner tiptoe through their own home-compounds everything else.

What troubles Alex most is the loss of autonomy they once took for granted. As a South Asian non-binary person, they'd already navigated complex questions of identity and belonging. They'd built a careful, deliberate life. Now they feel constantly monitored by their own nervous system, unable to trust their body's responses. A routine traffic stop-something millions of people experience without incident-has become a threshold they cannot cross without profound fear.

At work, Alex's performance has declined slightly, though they've managed to hide the worst of it. They've turned down a promotion because it would require more client-facing work, more unpredictability. They avoid going out, avoid driving when possible, avoid situations where they might encounter police. The world has become a place of careful calculations and hidden exits.

What Alex wants most is to feel safe again-not just physically, but in their own mind, in their own body. They want to stop scanning every environment for threat. They want to sleep without dread. They want their spouse to stop worrying. They want to reclaim the person they were before nine minutes changed everything.
